title: The spread of medical fake news in social media - the pilot quantitative study
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 80 most-shared Polish-language health links (top 10 for each of eight disease keywords, BuzzSumo, Aug 2012-Aug 2017), each link independently judged by two authors against an evidence-based internal-medicine textbook and coded fabricated / manipulated / advertisement / irrelevant / sufficient. The share of items classified as fake news is reported with its denominator ('40% of the studied material', N=80), which is a CONTENT prevalence estimate against an external ground truth. Not a classifier, intervention or belief study.

estimates.platform: Polish-language social media links indexed by BuzzSumo (Facebook engagements, Twitter, LinkedIn and Pinterest shares; Facebook accounted for 98-100% of total shares)
estimates.date: Links shared 1 August 2012 - 1 August 2017 (analysis conducted 2017; submitted 15 October 2017)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 80 most-shared Polish-language health web links (top 10 per disease keyword) whose content was classified as fake news (fabricated, manipulated or advertisement)
estimates.value_raw: "40% of the studied material" out of N=80 links; Table 1 per-keyword counts: cancer 5/10, neoplasm 2/10, diabetes 3/10, hypertension 7/10, vaccinations 9/10, HIV/AIDS 7/10 (AIDS 5/5, HIV 2/5), stroke 0/10, heart attack 0/10; fake-news links shared 451,272 times
estimates.denominator: 80 web links: the ten most-shared Polish-language pages for each of eight disease keywords (cancer/rak, neoplasm/nowotwor, heart attack/zawal, stroke/udar, hypertension/nadcisnienie, diabetes/cukrzyca, vaccinations/szczepienia, HIV and AIDS), filtered to 1 Aug 2012-1 Aug 2017
estimates.definition: A link counted in the numerator if its content fell in categories 1-3 of the authors' adapted Tandoc/Lim/Ling typology, pooled as 'fake news': (1) fabricated - completely fictitious medical facts or events; (2) manipulated - generally true basic information but false conclusions or recommendations from over-interpreted or overly extrapolated results; (3) advertisement - stories about diseases, often critical towards conventional therapies, designed to advertise 'miracle products'. Categories 4 (irrelevant) and 5 (sufficient) were not counted. Veracity was judged by comparison with 'Interna Szczeklika', a Polish evidence-based internal-medicine textbook.
estimates.misinfo_def: "It was defined as 'news that is intentionally false and could mislead readers' [5]"; operationally, "For purposes of the statistical analysis of this preliminary report, categories 1-3 were gathered together and marked as "fake news"."
estimates.n: 80 web links (10 per keyword x 8 keywords)
estimates.source_quote: Results: 40% of the most frequently shared links contained text we classified as fake news. These were shared more than 450,000 times.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); Results section and Table 1; Highlights
estimates.ground_truth_detail: "Each link was independently reviewed by two of the authors (PW and WKW)", both from a medical university, with veracity judged against the annually updated Polish evidence-based internal-medicine textbook 'Interna Szczeklika' (mp.pl/interna). Interobserver reliability: 90% observed agreement, Kappa = 0.875 (95% CI 0.838-0.912), SE of kappa = 0.019, weighted kappa = 0.890; inconsistent ratings re-reviewed and settled by consensus.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data was obtained for ten most commonly shared pages concerning eight keywords (N=80):
estimates.notes: Construct call: coded CONTENT, not SHARING, because the denominator is a set of 80 ITEMS each counted once (a rank-truncated top-10-per-keyword sample), not a volume of shares; popularity is only the selection mechanism, which the schema handles with denom_selection=curated. A SHARING content_share would need the fake-news share of total share volume - the paper gives 451,272 fake-news shares but total share volume only as per-keyword MEANS in thousands, so that figure cannot be built without computation (R8). Arithmetic check for an adjudicator: the Table 1 per-keyword counts sum to 33/80 = 41.3%, slightly above the stated 40% (32/80); I kept the paper's stated 40%. Country is coded Poland although the filter was LANGUAGE (Polish), not geography. platform_norm=web_cross_platform: the items are web articles, with sharing counted across Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn and Pinterest (Facebook 98-100%). breadth=misleading because the numerator pools fabricated content with 'manipulated' items whose basic information is true and with advertising, so it is the loosest veracity bar. Confidence medium: a self-described pilot (N=80), BuzzSumo unvalidated for medical research by the authors' own admission, keyword list without synonyms, and the 40%/41% discrepancy. Quote note: the text file is the ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT proof, whose diagonal 'ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT' watermark is rendered as letter fragments (CR / IP / T / AN / US / M / ED / PT / CE / AC) interleaved every second line, so most body sentences have no contiguous verbatim span. source_quote is therefore taken from the abstract, which renders cleanly; the Results section states the same figure as '2017 and accounted for 40% of the studied material (Table 1)' and the Discussion as 'In our material, 40% of the links were assessed as fake news.'

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) The per-keyword shares in Table 1 (vaccinations 9/10 = 90%, hypertension 7/10 = 70%, HIV/AIDS 7/10 = 70%, cancer 5/10 = 50%, diabetes 3/10 = 30%, neoplasm 2/10 = 20%, stroke 0/10 and heart attack 0/10 = 0%; abstract: 'The most fallacious content concerned vaccines' 90%, 'followed by hypertension and HIV/AIDS (both in 70%)'). These are topic subdivisions of the SAME 80-link corpus, and the row rule splits by country, platform or measure rather than by topic, so keeping them as rows would double-count the pooled 40%. They are listed here in full so an adjudicator can promote the vaccines (90%) cell if the project wants topic-level rows - each has an n of only 10 links. (b) 'Sufficient news represented only 19%' and the residual 'irrelevant' links: accuracy/off-topic shares, the mirror or remainder of the row kept, so not separate prevalence estimates. (c) CONCENTRATION not extracted although the study reports concentration in words: 'More than 20% of dangerous links from our material was generated by one source' and 'The publisher's website was also listed more times in the analysis and its links accounted for 94,000 cumulative shares (21% of all fake news)'. R1 fails: conc_share_pct is available (21% of fake-news shares) but conc_group_pct cannot be built - the group is 'one source' as a bare count and the total number of distinct sources in the corpus is never stated. It is also concentration WITHIN the misinformation subset (21% of fake-news shares, not of all exposure or sharing), a different quantity from population-level concentration. (d) The single most-shared link (a 'miracle cancer treatment' story, 'shared nearly 65,000 times') and the two example true videos (~5,500 and 21,600 shares) are single-item counts with no denominator. (e) Figures cited from other work in the Discussion (75% of Americans familiar with a fake story viewed it as accurate; 23% of Americans said they had shared a made-up story; ~half of Americans believe a medical conspiracy theory) are borrowed from elsewhere and barred by R8, and the last two are belief/self-report from other papers.

rob.design: Rank-truncated keyword sample of web content, no human subjects: BuzzSumo Enterprise 'Most Shared' queries for eight Polish disease keywords, filtered to Polish language and 1 Aug 2012-1 Aug 2017, retaining the top 10 links per keyword (N=80). Share metrics are BuzzSumo's Facebook engagements (likes+comments+shares) plus Twitter, LinkedIn and Pinterest shares; Facebook made up 98-100% of the total. Each link independently reviewed by two authors against the textbook 'Interna Szczeklika'; five content categories adapted from Tandoc, Lim & Ling (satire, parody and propaganda dropped as political and absent in screening), with categories 1-3 pooled as fake news. Reliability: 90% agreement, kappa = 0.875 (95% CI 0.838-0.912), weighted kappa = 0.890, disagreements resolved by consensus. No response rate (no participants); ethical approval not required. Authors' own stated limitations: BuzzSumo lacks validation in medical science ('a major weakness'), the fake-news typology is unvalidated, the search was 'rather preliminary and therefore, by definition, not extensive' using only direct terms with no synonyms or PRISMA-like procedure, so some top-shared articles may have been missed. Explicitly framed as a pilot study. Quote note: watermark fragments from the 'ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT' proof stamp are interleaved between body lines, so item6_quote is truncated at the watermark break; its full sentence reads 'For purposes of the statistical analysis of this preliminary report, categories 1-3 were gathered together and marked as "fake news".'

rob.item10_quote: In our material, 40% of the links were assessed as fake news.
